lead: A servlet is a Java class that answers HTTP requests inside a servlet container such as Tomcat. The container creates one object, calls init() once, service() for every request, and destroy() at shutdown. You write doGet() or doPost() to read parameters, headers and sessions, then write HTML or JSON back. This design gives Java web applications a single shared object with container-managed setup and cleanup. Servlets are the base under JSP, JSF and many Spring Boot request paths.
prereq: You need: Java classes and objects, the HTTP request and response model from Unit 1, Tomcat setup from 4.2, and session tracking from 4.6.

sections.h3: Life cycle: one object, many requests

blocks.text: A servlet is a Java object whose life the container controls. Tomcat loads the class and creates exactly one instance for a mapping. After construction, the container calls init(ServletConfig) once, before the first request. Put one-time setup there, such as a database pool or a configuration value. Then service() runs for every request. HttpServlet.service() reads the HTTP method and calls doGet(), doPost(), doPut() and so on. At shutdown or undeploy, destroy() runs once.

Map the servlet in code with @WebServlet("/greet"), or in web.xml with servlet and servlet-mapping entries. Older containers use javax.servlet imports. Newer containers use jakarta.servlet. A class with the wrong import package is not a servlet for that container and fails to load.

The container uses one thread per request on the one servlet object. Instance fields are shared by all those threads. A field such as String userName can show one user's data to another user. Keep per-request data in local variables or request attributes. Use a synchronized block only for a true shared counter, and expect lower throughput.

sections.h3: Reading a request and writing a response

blocks.text: Write a servlet by extending HttpServlet. The usual methods are protected void doGet(HttpServletRequest req, HttpServletResponse res) throws IOException, ServletException and the same signature for doPost. HttpServletRequest gives getParameter("name"), which returns a String or null. For an application/x-www-form-urlencoded form POST, Tomcat parses the body and getParameter still works. For multipart/form-data, add @MultipartConfig or read parts with getPart(). Use Integer.parseInt() for numbers. getParameter returns null if the parameter is missing, so check for null and catch NumberFormatException before using Integer.parseInt().

Read headers with getHeader("User-Agent") and the method with getMethod(). On the response, call setContentType("text/html;charset=UTF-8") before getWriter(). The writer is a PrintWriter; out.println() writes the body. setStatus(404) or sendError(404, "Not found") sets the status. Do not write to the writer after a forward.

GET puts data in the URL, so it suits reads and bookmarkable pages. POST puts data in the body, so it suits form submissions and changes. If a servlet overrides only doPost, a GET reaches the default doGet, which returns 405 Method Not Allowed. The client sends the HTTP method in the request line. service() reads it and dispatches to the matching doXxx() method; your code never calls doGet() or doPost() itself.

A forward stays on the server: req.getRequestDispatcher("/view.jsp").forward(req, res) sends the same request and response objects to another resource. The browser URL does not change. A redirect sends 302 to the browser: res.sendRedirect("next"). The browser makes a new request, the URL changes, and request attributes are lost. Use forward for MVC views; use redirect after a POST so refresh does not resubmit.

Init-params belong to one servlet: getServletConfig().getInitParameter("db"). Context-params belong to the whole web app: getServletContext().getInitParameter("db"). Init-params are set in web.xml or with @WebInitParam inside @WebServlet. Context-params have no annotation; set them in web.xml with <context-param>, or at startup in a ServletContextListener using getServletContext().setInitParameter(). Both reach your code as strings.

For login state use HttpSession session = req.getSession(true), then session.setAttribute("user", name). The session ID travels in a cookie, as in 4.6. Session attributes are shared across requests from the same browser, so guard mutable objects. Remove with removeAttribute or invalidate() at logout.

spec.aria: A timeline: load and create, init once, three service calls each leading to doGet printing Anu scored 78, then destroy once.

examples.question: A GreetServlet is mapped to /greet. It reads name=Anu and marks=78. Give the doGet body and trace the life cycle for three identical GET requests. State the exact output for one request and the number of init(), service() and destroy() calls. The small class below simulates what the container does so you can see the call order. The real servlet extends HttpServlet and its doGet takes HttpServletRequest and HttpServletResponse, as shown in step 3.
steps: The container loads GreetServlet and creates one instance.
It calls init() once. No request data is stored in an instance field.

In doGet: String name = req.getParameter("name"); int marks = Integer.parseInt(req.getParameter("marks")); res.setContentType("text/html;charset=UTF-8"); PrintWriter out = res.getWriter(); out.println(name + " scored " + marks);.
Request 1: name is Anu, marks is 78, output is Anu scored 78.
Requests 2 and 3 repeat the same service() and doGet() calls with the same values.
examples.answer: One request prints Anu scored 78; across three requests init() runs 1 time, service() runs 3 times, and destroy() runs 1 time.

n_requests = 3
marks = 78

print(n_requests)

traps: Putting per-user data in an instance field of the servlet. The container has one servlet object, so all requests share that field.
Expecting doPost to run for a GET. service() dispatches by HTTP method, and the default doGet returns 405.
Calling getWriter() before setContentType(). Set the content type and charset first.
Confusing forward with sendRedirect. Forward keeps the URL and request attributes; redirect starts a new request in the browser.
Mixing javax.servlet and jakarta.servlet imports. A container accepts only one package name.

quiz.q: Which servlet method runs exactly once after the object is created and before the first request?
Why does a servlet usually avoid mutable instance fields for per-user data?
quiz.a: The container has one servlet instance and serves requests on many threads. A shared field can mix one user's data into another user's response. Use local variables, request attributes or session attributes.

quiz.q: A servlet is mapped to /hi. A request is /hi?name=Ravi. Complete the line that prints Hi Ravi.
A servlet overrides only doPost. A browser sends GET /save. What response comes?
quiz.a: 405 Method Not Allowed. service() dispatches a GET to doGet, and the default doGet sends 405.
Forward runs on the server with the same request and keeps the URL. Redirect sends 302 and the browser makes a new request with a new URL.

quiz.q: Write the call that reads an init-param named db from inside a servlet.
Two threads run a servlet method that does count++ on an instance field without synchronization. What can go wrong?
quiz.a: The read-modify-write can interleave. Both threads may read the same old value, so one increment is lost and the count is too small. Use AtomicInteger or synchronize.

beyond: Not for the exam. Spring Boot wraps a servlet container and routes requests through DispatcherServlet, but singleton beans still face the same shared-state rule. Servlet filters and listeners add cross-cutting work such as logging, compression and security. Virtual threads change the cost of blocking calls, not the HTTP contract. Search next: Jakarta Servlet 6, Tomcat threading, RequestDispatcher, servlet filters.
